questions.stem: The most ABUNDANT gas in the Earth's atmosphere by volume is:

options.option_text: NITROGEN (N₂) — ~78.09% by volume; inert diatomic molecule with a very strong triple bond (bond energy 946 kJ/mol)

questions.explanation: EARTH'S ATMOSPHERE composition (by volume, in dry air): (1) NITROGEN N₂ — 78.09%; (2) OXYGEN O₂ — 20.95%; (3) ARGON Ar — 0.93%; (4) CARBON DIOXIDE CO₂ — 0.042% (420+ ppm, 2024); (5) TRACES of Neon, Helium, Methane CH₄, Krypton, Hydrogen, Xenon, Nitrous oxide N₂O, Ozone O₃. WATER VAPOUR is variable (0-4%). NITROGEN — diatomic molecule N≡N with very STRONG triple bond (946 kJ/mol), making it EXTREMELY UNREACTIVE at ordinary temperatures. Despite abundance, N₂ is unusable directly by most organisms. Must be ‘FIXED’ (converted to NH₃ or nitrates) by: (a) BIOLOGICAL FIXATION — symbiotic Rhizobium bacteria in leguminous root nodules; cyanobacteria (BGA — blue-green algae) like Anabaena, Nostoc; free-living soil bacteria Azotobacter, Clostridium; (b) LIGHTNING FIXATION — atmospheric N₂ + O₂ under lightning discharge → NO → NO₂ → HNO₃ (rain → soil nitrates); minor but historically important (few kg N/hectare/year); (c) INDUSTRIAL — HABER-BOSCH PROCESS (1908-13): N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ at high T + P over Fe catalyst; produces ammonia → fertilisers; feeds ~half the world. USES OF NITROGEN: (1) in fertilisers — urea (CO(NH₂)₂, 46% N, world's most used fertiliser), ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate, DAP, NPK; (2) PACKAGING — inert atmosphere for food packaging (chips, snacks) to prevent oxidation + rancidity; (3) LIQUID NITROGEN (boiling point -196°C) — cryogenic cooling (superconducting magnets in MRI, semiconductor industry, biological preservation of sperm/ova/tissue), food freezing, cryotherapy for warts; (4) TYRE INFLATION — more stable pressure under temperature variation than air; used in F1 + aviation; (5) FLUSHING INDUSTRIAL PIPELINES; (6) EXPLOSIVES — TNT (trinitrotoluene), RDX (cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine), PETN, dynamite. NITROGEN COMPOUNDS of EXAM interest: (a) NH₃ (ammonia) — pungent gas, key industrial chemical; (b) HNO₃ (nitric acid) — strong oxidising acid, manufactured by OSTWALD process (4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O → 2NO₂ → HNO₃ via Pt catalyst); used in fertilisers + explosives; (c) N₂O (nitrous oxide / LAUGHING GAS) — anaesthetic, whipped cream propellant, GHG (298x CO₂); (d) NO (nitric oxide) — signalling molecule in biology (1998 Medicine Nobel to Furchgott+Ignarro+Murad); (e) NO₂ (nitrogen dioxide) — brown toxic gas, vehicle exhaust + power plant, contributes to photochemical smog + acid rain; (f) NH₄NO₃ (ammonium nitrate) — fertiliser + explosive (Oklahoma City 1995, Beirut 2020); (g) DYNAMITE — nitroglycerin absorbed on diatomaceous earth (Nobel, 1867); (h) AZIDE NaN₃ — airbag propellant. NITROGEN CYCLE — see Environment book: fixation → nitrification (Nitrosomonas: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻; Nitrobacter: NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻) → assimilation by plants → ammonification (decay) → denitrification (Pseudomonas: NO₃⁻ → N₂ back to atmosphere).

questions.stem: The only NON-METAL that is LIQUID at room temperature is:

options.option_text: BROMINE (Br₂) — reddish-brown, fuming, toxic liquid; melts at -7.2°C, boils at 58.8°C; one of only 2 LIQUID ELEMENTS at room temperature (the other is MERCURY, a metal)

questions.explanation: BROMINE (Br₂, atomic number 35) — a HALOGEN (group 17); at room temperature, it is a DEEP REDDISH-BROWN LIQUID that FUMES (evaporates easily). ONLY NON-METAL ELEMENT LIQUID at room temperature (25°C). Other LIQUID ELEMENTS at room temperature: MERCURY (Hg) — only liquid METAL; and close-to-liquid are CAESIUM (Cs, m.p. 28.4°C, liquid in tropical summer), GALLIUM (Ga, m.p. 29.8°C, melts in warm hand), RUBIDIUM (Rb, m.p. 39.3°C), FRANCIUM (m.p. ~27°C, but radioactive + extremely rare). DISCOVERY of BROMINE: 1826 by ANTOINE JÉRÔME BALARD (French chemist, age 24, working in Montpellier; obtained it from seaweed ash + later from bittern of sea salt brines). Independently by CARL JACOB LÖWIG in Germany. NAMED from Greek ‘bromos’ = ‘stench’ (intensely pungent smell). OCCURRENCE: mainly as BROMIDE SALTS in seawater (65 ppm); in brines of DEAD SEA (Israel-Jordan, 0.8% Br), Mediterranean, Arkansas (USA); some in Indian salt production at GUJARAT+TN coasts. Commercially extracted by oxidation of Br⁻ with Cl₂: 2NaBr + Cl₂ → 2NaCl + Br₂. HAZARDS: highly TOXIC + CORROSIVE; causes burns, respiratory damage; vapour 3.1× denser than air, settles in low areas. USES: (1) Fire retardants — brominated compounds in plastics, textiles (but some banned — PBDEs persistent pollutants). (2) Photography — SILVER BROMIDE (AgBr) in traditional B&W film emulsions (along with AgCl, AgI); this use declined with digital. (3) Pharmaceuticals — potassium bromide (KBr) was historically used as anti-epileptic / sedative (hence Victorian ‘take a bromide’); still veterinary use. (4) Drilling fluids — dense bromide brines (ZnBr₂, CaBr₂). (5) Water treatment — as BrO⁻ or BCDMH for swimming pools, hot tubs (less harsh than chlorine). (6) Agrochemicals — methyl bromide fumigant (largely banned under Montreal Protocol as ozone-depleting). (7) Gasoline additive — ethylene dibromide was scavenger in leaded gasoline (phased out). HALOGEN group (Group 17): FLUORINE (F₂, pale yellow gas, MOST ELECTRONEGATIVE element; MOST REACTIVE of all non-metals; found in fluorite CaF₂ + fluorapatite; added to water + toothpaste as fluoride for teeth; HF etches glass; Teflon PTFE non-stick); CHLORINE (Cl₂, pale green pungent gas; used to kill bacteria in drinking water + swimming pools; making PVC; bleaching powder CaOCl₂; HCl in gastric juice; mustard gas C4H8Cl2S is WWI chemical weapon); BROMINE (as above); IODINE (I₂, purple-black solid, sublimes to violet vapour; in seaweed, potassium iodide added to TABLE SALT to prevent goitre from iodine deficiency; tincture of iodine antiseptic; radioactive I-131 for thyroid imaging/treatment; I-127 is stable isotope). ASTATINE (At, extremely rare, radioactive). TENNESSINE (Ts, synthetic, 2010). All halogens form HALIDE SALTS with alkali metals (NaCl, KBr, etc.) and HALOGEN ACIDS with hydrogen (HF, HCl, HBr, HI).

questions.stem: Of the following, which NON-METAL has the HIGHEST MELTING POINT and is the HARDEST natural substance?

options.option_text: DIAMOND (allotrope of CARBON) — m.p. ~3,550°C; HARDEST natural substance (10 on Mohs scale); tetrahedral sp³ covalent network; high refractive index (2.42); UNIQUE non-metal exception to the rule that non-metals are soft + low-melting

questions.explanation: DIAMOND — one of the ALLOTROPES of CARBON (the others: graphite, fullerenes, graphene, amorphous carbon, carbon nanotubes, carbyne, lonsdaleite). Diamond's UNIQUE properties make it an EXCEPTION to the general rule that non-metals are soft + low-melting: (1) HARDEST known NATURAL material (10 on Mohs scale); (2) HIGHEST MELTING POINT among non-metals (m.p. ~3,550°C, even higher under high pressure); (3) BEST NATURAL THERMAL CONDUCTOR (5× better than copper at room T); (4) high REFRACTIVE INDEX (2.42) — causes the characteristic SPARKLE / ‘fire’ from TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION + dispersion of white light into rainbow colours; (5) densest form of carbon (3.52 g/cm³); (6) transparent to UV + visible; (7) ELECTRICAL INSULATOR (despite being carbon); (8) CHEMICALLY INERT — resistant to acids; burns in O₂ only at >700°C. STRUCTURE of DIAMOND: each carbon atom forms FOUR sp³ COVALENT BONDS with 4 neighbouring carbons in a TETRAHEDRAL arrangement; extends in all 3 dimensions creating a RIGID CRYSTAL lattice with NO WEAK DIRECTIONS — hence hardness + hardness anisotropy. NATURAL DIAMONDS formed in the Earth's MANTLE under extreme pressure (>45 kbar) + heat (>900°C) at depths of 140-190 km, over millions of years. Brought to surface by deep-volcanic KIMBERLITE PIPES (named after Kimberley, South Africa — major source). MAJOR PRODUCERS today: Russia (largest, Alrosa), Botswana (Debswana, GEM quality), Canada, DR Congo, Australia (Argyle — famous for pink diamonds, closed 2020), South Africa. INDIA's DIAMOND HISTORY: (a) KIMBERLEY/GOLCONDA diamonds of AP-Telangana (Raichur doab) were the world's only source for ~1,800 years till Brazilian + African discoveries; (b) FAMOUS Indian diamonds: KOH-I-NOOR (‘Mountain of Light’, 105.6 carats now, taken by British 1849 from Lahore after Sikh war; mounted in Queen Mother's Crown, at Tower of London), HOPE DIAMOND (45.5 ct blue, now at Smithsonian — allegedly cursed), REGENT (140 ct), NASSAK, ORLOFF, DARYA-I-NOOR (‘Sea of Light’, Iran), PITT; (c) Indian DIAMOND CUTTING industry — SURAT, GUJARAT — cuts 90% of world's small diamonds; turnover $25B+. OTHER CARBON ALLOTROPES: (1) GRAPHITE — hexagonal sheets, weak inter-layer forces → soft, slippery, good lubricant (+conducts electricity — electrodes, pencils). (2) FULLERENES (C₆₀ ‘buckminsterfullerene’ — 1985 Nobel Kroto, Curl, Smalley; shaped like soccer ball; superconductors, drug delivery). (3) CARBON NANOTUBES (1991 Iijima) — cylindrical rolled graphene; ultra-strong, conductive, 100x steel strength. (4) GRAPHENE (2004 Geim + Novoselov, Nobel 2010) — single atomic layer of graphite; strongest material ever measured, transparent, highly conductive, 200× stronger than steel; huge future potential. (5) AMORPHOUS CARBON — charcoal, soot, lampblack. SYNTHETIC DIAMONDS: produced by (a) HIGH PRESSURE HIGH TEMPERATURE (HPHT, mimics Earth, since 1955 GE); (b) CHEMICAL VAPOUR DEPOSITION (CVD, from methane gas on a seed crystal) — 2020s trend: lab-grown diamonds identical to natural; increasingly popular + cheaper. India is a major CVD diamond producer/exporter. USES of DIAMOND: (i) JEWELLERY (80% of natural, by value); (ii) ABRASIVE + CUTTING tools — drill bits, saw blades, surgical scalpels; (iii) HEAT SINKS in electronics; (iv) HIGH-PRESSURE ANVIL cells in research; (v) optical windows; (vi) quantum computing (NV centres). DIAMOND CARAT = 200 mg = 0.2 g.

questions.stem: Which of the following gases is used to extinguish fires in LARGE ELECTRICAL / COMPUTING EQUIPMENT (e.g., data centres)?
questions.explanation: FIRE EXTINGUISHING — fire requires the ‘FIRE TRIANGLE’: FUEL + OXYGEN + HEAT (some add 4th element — CHEMICAL CHAIN REACTION — ‘fire tetrahedron’). REMOVE any one → fire goes out. For ELECTRICAL / ELECTRONIC equipment (servers, data centres, museum archives, aircraft), WATER + FOAM are UNSUITABLE: (a) water conducts electricity — shock risk + short circuits; (b) leaves residue damaging sensitive electronics + paper records; (c) can spread some burning liquids. PREFERRED EXTINGUISHING AGENTS for these environments: (1) CO₂ — CARBON DIOXIDE GAS: displaces oxygen below ~15%, suffocating the fire; colourless, odourless, non-conductive, leaves no residue; rapidly disperses. STANDARD CO₂ FIRE EXTINGUISHERS are black-banded in India (earlier entirely red, BIS IS 15683). Drawbacks: (a) lowers oxygen, dangerous for humans in enclosed spaces; (b) short-term cooling effect only. (2) DRY POWDER (Class A/B/C multi-purpose — sodium bicarbonate NaHCO₃, potassium bicarbonate KHCO₃, or monoammonium phosphate NH₄H₂PO₄). For class A (solid), B (liquid), C (gas) fires. Leaves residue. (3) CLEAN AGENTS — halocarbons + inert gas mixtures: (a) HALONS — Halon 1211 (BCF), Halon 1301 (BTM) — super-effective but BANNED under MONTREAL PROTOCOL as OZONE-DEPLETING; still used in critical aerospace + military till phase-out; replacements mandated since 1994. (b) HFC-227ea (HEPTAFLUOROPROPANE, FM-200) — widely used for data centre rooms; rapid discharge; no residue; breathable at design concentration. But is a GHG. (c) HFC-125, NOVEC 1230 (fluoroketone, 3M, low GWP, Tesla uses it for lithium battery fire). (d) INERGEN (IG-541) — mixture of 52% N₂ + 40% Ar + 8% CO₂; suppresses combustion while keeping air still breathable. (e) ARGONITE / IG-55 — 50% N₂ + 50% Ar. (f) IG-100 — pure N₂. (g) IG-01 — pure Ar. (4) WATER MIST — fine water droplets convert to steam, cool + displace oxygen; used on ships. FIRE CLASSES (most countries): CLASS A — solid materials (paper, wood, textiles) — water, foam; Class B — flammable liquids (petrol, oil) — foam, CO₂, dry powder; Class C — flammable gases — dry powder, water spray; Class D — combustible metals (Mg, Na, K, Al) — special dry powder (graphite, sodium chloride); Class E — electrical — CO₂, dry powder, clean agents; Class F/K — cooking oils/fats — wet chemical, foam. WATER vs GREASE FIRE: NEVER pour water on oil fires — causes massive flare-up (steam ejects hot oil). Smother with lid, use Class K extinguisher. COMMON EXTINGUISHER COLOUR (India, BIS): Red — Water / Class A; Cream — Foam / Class B; Black — CO₂ / electrical; Blue — dry powder; Yellow — wet chemical. (UK: red body, coloured band; USA: all red with label). displace oxygen without damaging equipment or leaving residue; safer than water/foam for live electronics; Argon, Nitrogen, mixtures like INERGEN.

questions.stem: SULPHUR occurs commonly in nature in several ALLOTROPES. Its most stable allotrope at room temperature is:
questions.explanation: SULPHUR (S, atomic number 16, group 16 Chalcogens) — known to ancients as ‘BRIMSTONE’. YELLOW solid at room temp; insoluble in water; soluble in CS₂. Exists in many ALLOTROPES (structural variants): (1) RHOMBIC / α-SULPHUR — YELLOW, brittle, octahedral/rhombic crystals; density 2.06; m.p. 112.8°C; MOST STABLE below 96°C; composed of PUCKERED CROWN-SHAPED S₈ RINGS. (2) MONOCLINIC / β-SULPHUR — needle-like, pale-yellow crystals; formed when rhombic is heated above 96°C; m.p. 119°C; stable between 96 and 119°C; also S₈ rings but packed differently. (3) PLASTIC / γ-SULPHUR — amorphous, dark-amber, rubbery; formed by rapidly cooling boiling S (~444°C) in cold water; S atoms form LONG CHAIN polymers; unstable, reverts to rhombic over time. (4) MILK OF SULPHUR / colloidal — fine yellow powder. OCCURRENCE: free in NATURE as S₈ (volcanic regions — Sicily, Texas, USA; once mined near Mount Etna); as SULPHIDES (pyrite FeS₂ ‘fool's gold’, galena PbS, chalcopyrite CuFeS₂, cinnabar HgS, stibnite Sb₂S₃); as SULPHATES (gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O, barite BaSO₄, epsom salt MgSO₄·7H₂O); in organic matter (proteins — amino acids cysteine + methionine; coal, petroleum); in HUMAN BODY (~140 g in adult, 3rd most common element after Ca, P). FRASCH PROCESS (1891 by Herman Frasch) — earlier main method: superheated steam (165°C) pumped into underground sulphur deposits; sulphur melts + rises via air-lift; cooled on surface — 99.9% pure. Nowadays, ~90% of industrial S is RECOVERED as by-product from desulphurisation of oil+gas (CLAUS process). USES: (1) SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄) — ‘KING OF CHEMICALS’; most produced industrial chemical; CONTACT PROCESS uses V₂O₅ catalyst: S + O₂ → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄. Uses: fertilisers (SSP single superphosphate, DAP diammonium phosphate), lead-acid batteries, detergents, petroleum refining, explosives, dye/pigments. H₂SO₄ is 80% of sulphur's use. (2) GUNPOWDER — 75% KNO₃ + 15% charcoal + 10% SULPHUR (ancient Chinese, 9th c.); used in fireworks, pyrotechnics. (3) MATCHES — red P + KClO₃ + S for striking head. (4) RUBBER VULCANISATION — Charles Goodyear 1839; heating rubber + sulphur → strong cross-linked elastic rubber (essential for car tyres, industrial rubber). (5) FUNGICIDE + INSECTICIDE — lime-sulphur spray. (6) MEDICINE — Ayurvedic ‘gandhaka’; antibiotic sulfa drugs (sulphonamides) like sulphanilamide — first large class of antibiotics (1935, Prontosil, Domagk Nobel 1939); acne cream. (7) BLACK GUNPOWDER + FIREWORKS pyrotechnics. (8) HYDROGEN SULPHIDE H₂S — rotten-egg smell; volcanic vents; toxic (more lethal than HCN at higher conc). (9) SO₂ — used as PRESERVATIVE (E220) in wine, dried fruits; bleaching wool + silk; dressing of jute. SULPHUR-containing amino acids: CYSTEINE (forms disulphide bridges stabilising proteins like insulin, keratin in hair/nails — that is why burnt hair has characteristic S smell), METHIONINE (start codon translation). HAIR PERMS — reshape by breaking + reforming disulphide bonds. yellow, brittle crystals; puckered S₈ rings; m.p. 113°C; most stable below 96°C; transitions to monoclinic above that.

questions.stem: PHOSPHORUS in the form of WHITE PHOSPHORUS (P₄) is:

options.option_text: Extremely REACTIVE + TOXIC + SELF-IGNITES in AIR above 34°C
The most abundant form in nature

questions.explanation: PHOSPHORUS (P, Z=15, group 15 Pnictogens). DISCOVERED 1669 by HENNIG BRAND (German alchemist) while experimenting with URINE (boiled 50 buckets down to a paste, distilled → glowed in dark — white phosphorus); 1st element discovered since prehistoric times; name from Greek ‘phos’ = light + ‘phoros’ = bearing (‘light-bearer’). Several ALLOTROPES: (1) WHITE PHOSPHORUS (WP, α-P₄) — colourless/yellow waxy SOLID; highly REACTIVE + TOXIC; bursts into flame spontaneously above 34°C in AIR (pyrophoric); stored UNDER WATER; emits faint green glow in dark (PHOSPHORESCENCE from slow oxidation to P₂O₃); extremely poisonous (lethal dose ~50 mg); causes ‘PHOSSY JAW’ (necrosis of jaw bone) — historical occupational disease in match-factory workers (19th c.). Used in military as INCENDIARY WEAPON (WP shells, smoke screens) — controversial under international humanitarian law due to burning injuries. Historic use in matches (dangerous, banned for safety — now red P used). WP has a tetrahedral P₄ molecular structure. (2) RED PHOSPHORUS — polymeric (chains of P atoms); dark red powder; NON-TOXIC + STABLE; ignition point ~260°C. Used in: (a) SAFETY MATCHES (on the striking surface; head contains KClO₃ + S + glass powder + glue); rubbed on red P strip → friction ignites P → heat ignites match head — invented 1855. (b) fireworks, smoke bombs; flame retardants; methamphetamine precursor (regulated). (3) BLACK PHOSPHORUS — LAYERED structure similar to graphite; MOST STABLE allotrope but requires high pressure to form; similar to 2D material like graphene — new research interest for electronics + batteries. (4) VIOLET PHOSPHORUS — crystalline; another stable allotrope. USES OF PHOSPHORUS (element): (1) FERTILISERS — P is one of 3 main plant macronutrients (NPK); as PHOSPHATE ROCK (Ca₃(PO₄)₂, fluorapatite) → processed to SUPERPHOSPHATE (Ca(H₂PO₄)₂) + TRIPLE SUPERPHOSPHATE + DAP (diammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₂HPO₄). Largest P use. (2) DETERGENTS (earlier — STPP, sodium tripolyphosphate; now restricted due to eutrophication). (3) MATCHES (red P). (4) FIREWORKS. (5) MILITARY — WP incendiaries. (6) PHARMACEUTICALS — metabolism-related drugs. (7) SOFT DRINKS — H₃PO₄ (phosphoric acid) in cola for tartness. (8) PHOSPHATE BUFFERS in biological labs. BIOLOGICAL ROLES — phosphorus is ESSENTIAL for life: (a) DNA + RNA backbones (phosphodiester bonds between nucleotides); (b) ATP — adenosine triphosphate, the ENERGY CURRENCY of cells (3 phosphate groups; hydrolysis of one phosphate releases ~30 kJ/mol of energy for cellular work); (c) BONES + TEETH — 85% of body's P is in bones as hydroxyapatite Ca₅(PO₄)₃(OH); (d) PHOSPHOLIPIDS of CELL MEMBRANES (bilayer, phosphate head + lipid tail); (e) PHOSPHORYLATION (adding phosphate) is a key regulatory mechanism for enzymes + proteins. DEFICIENCY: weak bones, fatigue, muscle weakness. Mostly sufficient in normal diet (meat, dairy, fish, nuts, pulses). PHOSPHATE ROCK is a FINITE RESOURCE — the P nutrient cycle does not have atmospheric fixation like N; concerns about ‘PEAK PHOSPHORUS’ (may run out in 50-100 years based on current consumption). 85% of world's phosphate rock is in MOROCCO (incl. occupied Western Sahara); other top producers: China, USA (Florida), Russia, Jordan. stored UNDER WATER; used in matches + incendiary weapons; red allotrope is safer and is the match-striking powder.

questions.stem: Of the NOBLE GASES (group 18), which one is used to fill LIGHT BULBS (incandescent + fluorescent) and in WELDING to provide an inert atmosphere?
questions.explanation: ARGON (Ar, Z=18, Group 18 Noble Gases) — Greek ‘argos’ = ‘inactive’. Discovered 1894 by LORD RAYLEIGH + WILLIAM RAMSAY (Nobel Chemistry 1904) by comparing air-derived N₂ with chemically-prepared N₂ and finding a density discrepancy → a new heavier inert gas. First noble gas discovered. ABUNDANCE: 3rd MOST ABUNDANT gas in Earth's atmosphere (~0.93% by volume); more abundant than CO₂. Produced mainly by RADIOACTIVE DECAY of ⁴⁰K (potassium-40) in Earth's crust → ⁴⁰Ar → atmosphere. Argon is 99.6% ⁴⁰Ar. PROPERTIES: colourless, odourless, tasteless, non-flammable, INERT (doesn't form stable compounds under normal conditions; only fragile HArF known, 2000 discovery). Boiling point -186°C. Density ~1.4× that of air. USES (why ARGON dominates industrial inert applications): (1) INCANDESCENT LIGHT BULBS — the glass envelope is filled with mixture of ARGON (93%) + a little NITROGEN; prevents the tungsten filament from OXIDISING + REDUCES EVAPORATION of W (high-T sublimation) → extends bulb life; ditto for FLUORESCENT + CFL bulbs (Ar + Hg vapour). (2) WELDING SHIELDING GAS — TIG (tungsten inert gas), MIG (metal inert gas) welding use pure Ar or Ar-CO₂ mix to protect the weld pool from oxygen + nitrogen of atmosphere; essential for stainless steel, aluminum, titanium welding. (3) METAL PROCESSING — Ar atmosphere for Ti + Zr + W production (these otherwise react with O₂ + N₂). (4) PRESERVATION — protective atmosphere for old/archival documents (National Archives, USA); wine preservation after opening; food packaging; pharmaceutical manufacture. (5) SEMICONDUCTOR industry — during silicon crystal growth, inert atmosphere. (6) CRYOGENIC coolant (though liquid N₂ cheaper). (7) SCUBA DIVING — argon in dry suits for insulation. (8) DOUBLE-PANE WINDOWS — Ar between glass panes improves thermal insulation (lower conduction than air). NOBLE GASES (Group 18) — HELIUM, NEON, ARGON, KRYPTON, XENON, RADON, + synthetic OGANESSON (2006, discovered in Dubna Russia, element 118 — completes period 7). WHY ‘NOBLE’? Full valence shell (ns²np⁶, 8 electrons; helium is 1s²), making them extremely UNREACTIVE. Some rare compounds formed with F, O under forcing conditions (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeO₃, KrF₂ — predicted impossible till 1962 by Neil Bartlett's Xe[PtF₆]). HELIUM (He, Z=2) — 2nd lightest element; UNIVERSE'S 2nd MOST ABUNDANT (24%, formed in Big Bang + stellar fusion); on Earth RARE (from radioactive α decay in crust, extracted from natural gas in Texas, USA + Qatar + Russia + Algeria); used in BALLOONS (non-flammable, unlike H₂ which caused Hindenburg 1937), MRI MAGNETS (liquid He coolant, -269°C, superconducting magnets), DEEP-SEA DIVING (mixed with O₂ as heliox to avoid nitrogen narcosis), ROCKETS (pressurising fuel tanks), WELDING of aluminium, leak detection, LAB cryogenics. Helium speaks ‘squeaky’ because sound travels faster in lighter gas. LIMITED SUPPLY concerns — cosmic helium lost to space, not renewable on Earth. NEON (Ne, Z=10) — ‘NEW’; in NEON SIGNS (red-orange glow); TV displays; cryogenics (-246°C). KRYPTON (Kr, 36) — flash lamps, some lasers. XENON (Xe, 54) — photography flash, high-intensity searchlights, car headlights (HID Xenon lamps), ION PROPULSION in spacecraft, general anaesthetic, excimer lasers (XeCl, XeF). RADON (Rn, 86) — radioactive; seeps into basements in some areas → LUNG CANCER risk; naturally from U decay. Ramsay won 1904 Chemistry Nobel for discovering several noble gases. 3rd most abundant gas in atmosphere (0.93%); inert; inexpensive; fills incandescent bulbs (prevents W filament oxidation + sublimation) + arc welding shield (TIG, MIG); cryogenic applications.

questions.stem: Which gas is used to fill WEATHER BALLOONS, and why is it preferred over hydrogen?

options.option_text: HELIUM — because it is NON-FLAMMABLE (hydrogen is); lifting power ~92% of hydrogen's but safety-critical after accidents like HINDENBURG 1937
Argon — heavier than air, floats better

questions.explanation: HELIUM (He, Z=2) — used to fill WEATHER BALLOONS, blimps, zeppelins, scientific balloons (NASA stratospheric balloons), party balloons. REASONS for preferring HELIUM over HYDROGEN (even though H₂ is cheaper + gives slightly better LIFT — 1 L of H₂ lifts 1.114 g in air vs He 1.024 g): (1) NON-FLAMMABLE / INERT — He cannot burn or explode; H₂ is highly flammable + explosive in air (4-74% by volume). (2) SAFER — HINDENBURG DISASTER (6 May 1937, Lakehurst, New Jersey, USA): the German zeppelin LZ 129 Hindenburg, filled with 200,000 m³ of H₂, caught fire + exploded during landing, killing 36 of 97 people on board. Broadcast live on radio (famous ‘OH, THE HUMANITY!’ reportage by Herbert Morrison). This ended the commercial airship era. After WWII, Helium (under USA near-monopoly at the time) was made accessible for non-military use. Modern airships (Goodyear Blimp, Zeppelin NT, Sergey Brin's Pathfinder 1) use HELIUM. (3) LIFTING POWER DIFFERENCE is marginal (~8%); safety premium is huge. (4) WEATHER BALLOONS — launched ~1,000+ times/day worldwide by meteorological agencies (India Meteorological Department, NOAA, etc.) for ATMOSPHERIC DATA (temperature, humidity, pressure, wind profile) up to 30+ km altitude; carry RADIOSONDES that transmit real-time data; balloon expands + BURSTS at ceiling; data ends, package parachutes down. Rubber/latex balloons, He-filled. (5) PARTY BALLOONS — though arguably wasteful since He is a FINITE RESOURCE on Earth. OTHER HE USES: (a) MRI machines — liquid He (-269°C, boiling point) cools superconducting magnets of MRI + NMR spectrometers + particle accelerators (LHC at CERN uses 120 tonnes of liquid He). MRI requires a STEADY SUPPLY of He (quench = loss is disaster). (b) SCUBA DIVING ‘HELIOX / TRIMIX’ — He replaces N₂ in breathing gas for deep diving to avoid nitrogen narcosis (‘rapture of the deep’) + decompression sickness (‘the bends’) at depths >50 m. (c) LEAK DETECTION — He atoms are small + inert + rare in atmosphere; He-leak detectors are sensitive. (d) WELDING of aluminium/Mg/refractories. (e) GROWING SILICON CRYSTALS (semiconductor industry). (f) ROCKETS — SpaceX Falcon 9 uses He to pressurise LOX + RP-1 tanks. (g) LABORATORY cryogenics. HELIUM SUPPLY CRISIS: He is extracted from NATURAL GAS wells (0.3-7% He content, formed by radioactive decay deep underground); richest wells in USA (Amarillo, TX), QATAR, ALGERIA, RUSSIA (Amur project, Gazprom). US FEDERAL HELIUM RESERVE in Cliffside TX (largest in world, 1925 established for military airships; sale mandated 1996; finally privatised 2023). Concerns: He released to atmosphere is LOST to space (too light to retain); not renewable at human timescales. SCIENTIFIC COMMUNITY calls for restrictions on balloon/wasteful uses. INDIAN He: India imports nearly all its He; some extracted from natural gas (ONGC), but mostly imported. ISRO uses He in rockets (PSLV + GSLV stages). 2023 — HELIUM India Pvt Ltd started domestic purification. Hydrogen may return: 2020s — hybrid airships (Hindenburg-plus-safety) proposed with inert He outer lift + hot-air core.

questions.stem: OZONE (O₃) in the STRATOSPHERE (~20-30 km altitude) is beneficial because it:

options.option_text: Adds breathable oxygen to the atmosphere
Absorbs most of the Sun's HARMFUL ULTRAVIOLET (UV-B, UV-C) RADIATION
Regulates Earth's temperature via CO₂ buffering

questions.explanation: OZONE (O₃, ‘activated oxygen’) — an ALLOTROPE of OXYGEN consisting of 3 oxygen atoms in a bent triangular molecule (vs common O₂). TWO KEY atmospheric locations: (1) STRATOSPHERIC OZONE (the ‘OZONE LAYER’) at ~15-35 km altitude, concentrated around 20-30 km (Chapman cycle); BENEFICIAL — absorbs ~97-99% of the Sun's dangerous ULTRAVIOLET RADIATION (UV-B 280-315 nm + UV-C 100-280 nm); protects life from skin cancer, cataracts, immune suppression, DNA mutations, coral damage. (2) TROPOSPHERIC / GROUND-LEVEL OZONE (0-10 km, near surface) — HARMFUL pollutant; component of photochemical SMOG (formed by NOₓ + VOCs + sunlight); respiratory irritant, reduces lung function; damages plants + crops. Good ozone up high, bad ozone down low. OZONE LAYER DEGRADATION: discovered 1974 — MARIO MOLINA + F. SHERWOOD ROWLAND (both Nobel Chemistry 1995 with Paul Crutzen) showed that CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs — Cl₃CF, Cl₂CF₂, used since 1930s as refrigerants, aerosol propellants, foaming agents, solvents) release Cl radicals in the stratosphere on UV exposure; each Cl can CATALYTICALLY destroy ~100,000 ozone molecules. The ANTARCTIC OZONE HOLE was confirmed in 1985 by BRITISH ANTARCTIC SURVEY (Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin in Nature) — a massive thinning of ozone over Antarctica each spring (September-October). MONTREAL PROTOCOL on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, signed 16 September 1987, Montreal, Canada; entered force 1 Jan 1989; RATIFIED by 198 UN parties (the ONLY UN treaty ratified universally) → phased out CFCs, halons, methyl bromide, CCl₄, CH₃CCl₃. Developed nations banned by 1996; developing countries by 2010. Replacements: HCFCs (transitional, phasing out by 2030-2040); HFCs (no Cl, hence no ozone effect, but HIGH GWP greenhouse gases — being replaced under KIGALI AMENDMENT 2016 with HFOs + natural refrigerants like CO₂, NH₃, HCs). RESULT: ozone layer is RECOVERING — expected to fully heal by ~2040 (middle latitudes), 2045 (Arctic), 2066 (Antarctic per WMO 2022 assessment). The Montreal Protocol is the GREATEST ENVIRONMENTAL TREATY SUCCESS STORY — proof that collective global action works. 16 September = World Ozone Day. OTHER OZONE FACTS: (a) Pungent smell after thunderstorms (lightning creates O₃ from O₂); (b) USED in water + wastewater treatment as disinfectant (STRONGER oxidiser than Cl₂, no residue); (c) used to bleach paper, textiles; (d) industrial deodorisation; (e) atmospheric chemistry research; (f) MEDICINE — ozone therapy (controversial); (g) dangerous to humans at >0.1 ppm (lung irritant, edema). DOBSON UNIT (DU) — measurement of ozone column thickness; 1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0°C + 1 atm; normal ozone column ~300 DU; ozone hole when <220 DU; minimum over Antarctica reaches ~90 DU. OZONE + UV cycle: O₂ + UV (<242 nm) → 2O; O + O₂ → O₃; O₃ + UV (200-320 nm) → O₂ + O; continuous steady state. But Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂ — Cl catalyst not consumed, destroys ozone. protecting life from skin cancer, cataracts, DNA damage; measured in DOBSON UNITS.

questions.stem: CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) is a SILENT KILLER because it is:
questions.explanation: CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) — a COLOURLESS, ODOURLESS, TASTELESS, NON-IRRITATING, highly toxic gas. HIGHLY DANGEROUS because: (1) SENSORY EVASION — humans cannot detect it without instruments (no smell, no colour, no taste); VICTIMS often unaware until they collapse. (2) MECHANISM OF TOXICITY: CO binds to HAEMOGLOBIN (Hb) with an affinity 240× greater than O₂; forms CARBOXYHAEMOGLOBIN (COHb); red blood cells cannot release O₂ to tissues → HYPOXIA (oxygen starvation) → tissue damage → death. Even 0.04% CO in air can be lethal within hours. (3) ALSO inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria; binds myoglobin in muscles. Brain + heart most affected (high O₂ demand). SYMPTOMS: mild — headache, dizziness, nausea, fatigue (often mistaken for flu); moderate — confusion, vomiting, chest pain, drowsiness; severe — unconsciousness, seizures, coma, death. TREATMENT: remove from source + 100% oxygen (in severe cases hyperbaric oxygen therapy). SOURCES of CO: (1) INCOMPLETE COMBUSTION of carbon-containing fuels: gas geysers in poorly-ventilated bathrooms (major cause of bathroom deaths in India); vehicle exhausts (catalytic converters reduce CO → CO₂); kerosene stoves, portable heaters, charcoal grills, improperly vented fireplaces; (2) HOUSE FIRES (smoke kills by CO poisoning before flames); (3) INDUSTRIAL processes (blast furnaces for steel use CO as reducing agent: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂); (4) Cigarette smoke (contains 3-6% CO — chronic smokers have 5-10% COHb). ATMOSPHERIC CO — not a major greenhouse gas but PRECURSOR of ground-level ozone + methane. PREVENTION: install CO detector (alarms at 50-70 ppm); ventilate all combustion appliances; never run generators in closed spaces; annual inspection of gas appliances. INDIAN BUREAU of STANDARDS recommends CO detectors in homes with gas appliances. Signs: ‘GEYSER IN BATHROOM’ deaths regularly reported (Kerala, Goa, Delhi, Mumbai in winter — monsoon months closed ventilation). NFPA (USA) recommends <9 ppm as safe; >100 ppm = dangerous. CO as USEFUL: (1) METALLURGY — reducing agent in blast furnaces (extracting Fe from Fe₂O₃ since ancient times); (2) WATER GAS (CO + H₂) — produced by passing steam over red-hot coke; (3) PRODUCER GAS (CO + N₂) — from burning coke in limited air; used as industrial fuel; (4) FISCHER-TROPSCH process — CO + H₂ over Fe/Co catalyst → synthetic hydrocarbons (used by Germany in WWII, South Africa during apartheid-era oil embargo); (5) CARBONYL process — purification of Ni (metal + CO → Ni(CO)₄ → decomposed back to pure Ni, Mond process); (6) CARBONYLS — organometallic compounds widely used in industrial + lab chemistry; (7) ORGANIC CHEMISTRY — carbonylation reactions (hydroformylation, Reppe chemistry). CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂) vs CO — CO₂ is odourless + tasteless + colourless too BUT not toxic at normal levels (we exhale it); dangerous only at high concentrations (displaces O₂; >10% → unconsciousness; volcanic vents, LAKE NYOS 1986 disaster in Cameroon where 1,700 asphyxiated by CO₂ cloud from limnic eruption). CO₂ IS A GREENHOUSE GAS — primary driver of anthropogenic climate change. geysers, vehicles, heaters. binds HAEMOGLOBIN 240× STRONGER than O₂, forming CARBOXYHAEMOGLOBIN → oxygen starvation; victims die without realising; produced from INCOMPLETE combustion.
